body.speaker: Instructor
body.text:
Hi. This is the scenario-based activity on **Interdisciplinary Research Project**.

There are three parts. Each part should take around 45 minutes to an hour, and you can break it up over several days if you'd like. Part 1 is due November 15, 2026.

In this module, you'll complete Part 1 of a simulated project in which you’ll apply what you’ve learned in class about interdisciplinary analysis. The module contains everything you need to complete the project.

There are instructions on the screen to help you navigate and give your answers. There are also a few links embedded in the text. You can use them for additional information, but that’s optional.

Remember that I will be seeing these results, so please take it seriously and do your best work. I think you'll enjoy it.

Click the Continue button to start.

body.speaker: Instructor
body.text:
Imagine that as part of your degree requirements, you are completing an internship at a local nonprofit organization called **Community 360,** or **Comm360** for short.

The mission of Comm360 is to address **community-based needs and issues** through responsive programming in multiple areas such as:

- Education and Training
- Health and Wellness
- Family and Youth Services
- Community Building and Advocacy

A community needs survey conducted by Comm360 identified the high rate of housing insecurity, specifically homelessness, in the area as a serious issue. You have been asked to work with other interns to investigate the **causes of homelessness** to better understand the problem so that Comm360 can explore ways to address this problem.

body.speaker: Instructor
body.text:
Your intern teammates are **Ty, Peggy**, and **Lacy**.

The team is responsible for helping each other identify key concepts, review and learn from readings, and organize information.

**Lianne Park** is your Supervisor/Mentor at Comm360. She’s been there for five years and directs multiple programs. She will present your findings and work to the **Program Development & Evaluation (PDE) committee** for review.

Lianne reports to the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), **Anne Hastings**. Ms. Hastings makes the ultimate decisions about programs and resources.

body.speaker: Instructor
body.text:
Over three (3) parts of this Scenario-based Activity (SBA), you will work with your teammates to complete the following **Tasks**.

1. Brainstorm causes for homelessness.
1. Review community focus group data.
1. Reflect: Is this an Interdisciplinary Problem?
1. Review the literature.
1. Integrate disciplinary insights.
1. Help the nonprofit leadership share the results through public awareness.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Hey, team. We’re glad you’re here at Comm360 to help us work on this problem.

When people experience homelessness — whether short-term or long-term — it can affect their health, safety, employment, and overall stability.

We want to better understand the causes of homelessness.

Why don’t each of you start by reviewing what you already know about why people lose stable housing?

It may be from personal experiences, things you’ve seen in your community, or stories you’ve heard.

When you’re done, we’ll put all the ideas together as a way to start looking into research about the causes of homelessness.

By the way, you can call me Lianne. We’re pretty informal here.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: Thanks, Lianne. I’ve heard stories about people losing housing after medical bills or job loss, but I’ve never really thought about all the different reasons it might happen.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text:
Me too. Maybe we should each take a few minutes to think of different causes of homelessness.

When we’re done, we can start writing them down.

Then we can choose which ones might be most useful for researching the issue, like Lianne suggested.

I’m just not sure how to organize them.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text:
I’ll start.

Actually… this topic feels kind of personal to me.

When I was in middle school, my mom lost her job unexpectedly. We thought we’d be fine, but a few months later we were behind on rent. I remember my parents whispering at night about whether we’d have to move.

We didn’t end up on the street, but we stayed with my aunt for almost six months. I didn’t realize at the time how close we were to losing our housing completely.

It made me realize how quickly things can change.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Thank you for sharing that, Peggy.

What you described is something researchers often refer to as housing instability — situations where families are temporarily doubled up or at risk of losing housing.

Experiences like that remind us that homelessness isn’t always sudden or visible. Sometimes it’s the result of a series of economic shocks over time.

Let’s keep that in mind as we continue identifying causes.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text:
Yeah, thanks for sharing that, Peggy.

I think what stands out to me is how it wasn’t one dramatic event — it was a job loss, then falling behind on rent, then having to move in with family.

It makes me think that homelessness might not always start with someone “choosing” anything. Sometimes it’s just a chain of events.

Maybe we should add something like:

“Unexpected job loss without financial savings can lead to housing instability.”

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text:
That makes sense. It’s not just one thing — it’s how things build on each other.

I think we’re starting to see a pattern where people can lose housing even if they’re working or trying to stay on track.

Maybe we should each come up with one or two causes like that — short statements — and then put them together.

That might help us see the bigger picture.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text:
Yeah, I can add one.

Maybe something like:

“Rising rent combined with wages that don’t increase at the same rate can make it difficult for people to keep stable housing.”

body.speaker: Ty
body.text:
I’ll add another one too.

“Unexpected expenses, like medical bills or car repairs can lead to falling behind on rent.”

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: That’s a good plan, but keep in mind — not all causes are structural or systemic.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: What do you mean?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
For example, some people may experience challenges that make it harder to maintain stable housing over time.

That could include things like untreated mental health conditions, substance use, or difficulty maintaining steady employment.

In those cases, it’s not just about housing availability or wages — it’s also about individual circumstances that can affect stability.

That’s an example of an individual-level cause — something happening at the level of a person’s experiences or situation.

As we continue identifying causes, it’s important to consider both sides — not just systems, but also individual factors that might contribute.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: Ah, I see. So why don’t we each write one cause that focuses more on an individual situation and one that reflects a structural factor?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: That makes sense. I’m not totally sure I get the difference yet, but I’ll try.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: What causes people to experience homelessness?

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: Here are all of our reasons. Lianne, what do you think?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
This is a good list. It reflects a lot of what we heard in a focus group we conducted after we reviewed the results of our community needs survey.

We spoke to various stakeholders — people currently experiencing homelessness, service providers, business owners, and community members.

I’d like you to take a look at part of the transcript from that focus group to extract additional reasons, because this is an extremely complex problem — as you’ve already identified — with many interacting causes. As you read through the focus group transcript again, notice whether Peggy’s experience appears in what participants shared.

Please highlight any additional causes you see — especially those that reflect housing instability.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Please highlight any reasons that our participants gave for losing housing security or homelessness.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: I hope we get to work on focus groups here because that was really interesting. Here’s what I highlighted.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text:
I studied focus groups in my research methods class last year. We analyzed lots of transcripts. Ty, I’m taking your highlights and combining them with the reasons we already came up with. I re-worded some of them, but I think I’ve captured everything.

Here are all the reasons either we or the participants gave for homelessness.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Good work. This list reflects what we’ve heard in the community about this issue.

Now we need to turn our attention to the research. I think we should focus on a subset of these reasons. Which ones would you select to research? Please pick at least 3 but no more than 5.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: I agree with you on some of your choices. Why did you select that set?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
I appreciate the thoughtfulness you’ve shown on this issue, both as individuals and as a team.

I reviewed the reasons you put together with Ms. Hastings. We agree that this subset of causes are appropriate for us to consider as an organization to build programmatic outreach/solutions:

- Trauma people experience — domestic violence, family conflict, untreated mental health conditions–can leave them with disrupted employment, relationships, and stability leading to housing insecurity.
- In some places, limited economic opportunity — such as fewer job opportunities or restrictive labor market conditions — can make it harder for people to find and maintain stable employment, increasing the risk of homelessness.
- Racial discrimination in housing and lending markets can limit access to stable and affordable housing for some groups.
- Limited access to cash assistance or income support programs may leave vulnerable individuals and families without a financial safety net during crises.
- People who are unsheltered may face increased risks from extreme heat or severe weather, which can worsen health conditions and housing instability.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: This list cuts across a lot of different subjects. I’m looking forward to seeing what kind of research we’ll find for each of them.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Yes, and we’ll move into the research phase of this work shortly, but first I’d like us to discuss our approach. At Comm360, we typically use an interdisciplinary research process. In the past, this approach has allowed us to combine insights to come to a holistic solution for the issue we’re tackling.

So we’ll need to determine if the problem of people experiencing housing insecurity is the kind of problem that is appropriate for interdisciplinary research.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: According to the interdisciplinary research process model, we need to look at the causes on the list and see if they map to different disciplines.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text:
And we should identify the disciplines we think would give us the most useful insights into the problem.

Let’s do it.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text:
Let’s figure out which disciplines are likely to give us the most insights into the problem.

How about each of us select all the disciplines (in row) that we think apply for each of the causes listed?

I think it is OK if we check as many boxes in a row as we think apply.

Then, we can sum up our responses to see if they align and if we think this is an interdisciplinary problem.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text:
Ok, I summed up our responses and this shows any category that got more than one vote.

We didn’t always agree on each discipline, but overall we all seem to see how different disciplines might investigate the problem.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: I agree. Our analysis supports what you were saying, Ty. These causes cut across a lot of subjects.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: It seems like an interdisciplinary approach makes sense in this case.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I also agree. It’s a really complex problem, so the Interdisciplinary Research Process model should help Comm360 study it from a lot of different angles.

body.title: Task Set Four: Review the Literature

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
We all agree that taking an interdisciplinary approach will work to study a complex problem like housing insecurity.

Let’s dig in a bit now and get more information about some of the causes. We should be able to locate studies from some of the disciplines we have identified that address different parts of the problem.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: I’m already on it… I took a few key words from one of the causes and did a search. This study looks promising. Take a look.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: Here it is.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text:
This does look promising. Which discipline–or maybe disciplines–are represented in this study? I mean, which ones are the most relevant, if we have these to choose from?

Biology, Psychology, Earth science, Sociology, Economics, Political science, Public Policy, Social Work?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I think it’s Economics. There are some clues and jargon in the summary.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: Can you show us?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text:
So I highlighted the clues and jargon that make me think this study is mainly in the Economics.

For example, the authors keep focusing on ideas like “institutional economic hypotheses,” “labor market freedom,” “entrepreneurial activity,” and “economic opportunity.” Those are concepts economists often use when they study how larger economic systems influence people’s lives.

Another takeaway was that it is published in an economics journal. Applied Economics, to be specific.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Here, the major phenomena are **labor markets, entrepreneurship, economic opportunity, and employment.**

These are important clues to the Economics perspective this study brings to homelessness. Now let’s find out what the study concluded about them—its main insight.

The main insight is usually a study's **main finding, explanation, or recommendation**. That means some parts of the source will give us better clues than others.

Which sections do you think we should examine most closely?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: I agree with you on some of your choices. Why did you select that set?

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: I think Results is important because that's where we'll see what the researchers found.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: And I'd look closely at the Discussion and Conclusion; that's where authors explain what those findings mean.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Great. Let's look at those sections. Highlight 2–3 sentences that give us the strongest clues about the study's main insight.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: These are my highlights. I think these provide clues we need for this study’s main insight.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I highlighted these too. They tell us the study’s main findings, explain what those findings mean, and point to the larger conclusion the researchers draw from them. Those are exactly the kinds of clues we should look for when identifying a study’s main insight.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
These look great, everyone! Now look across the sentences you highlighted.

In your own words, what do you think is the **main insight of this study?**

Try to capture more than a single result. Think about what the researchers want us to understand from the study as a whole.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Good work. Here are the sentences you all suggested. Which one should we go with?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: You chose the following sentence. Why did you select that one?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
I agree with those of you who selected this sentence as the study's main insight.

**Higher levels of entrepreneurial activity and labor market freedom may reduce homelessness by expanding economic opportunity and reducing barriers to employment.**

This insight reflects the Economics perspective because it explains homelessness in terms of markets, economic opportunity, and employment rather than individual circumstances or public programs.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: In fact, we should start a table of study elements. We can use this table to compare disciplinary perspectives of studies we review. A discipline’s perspective is influenced by the elements you see in this table. I went ahead and included the phenomena studied in this study as well as its main insight. Let’s locate the other elements from the study.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: Great! Let’s start with Questions Asked. Why don’t we look in the source text and see if we can locate information that we can use.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: That is a great idea. I don’t see research questions mentioned explicitly in the study but there is information in the Abstract and Introduction sections, and even the Background section, that can be helpful.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I glanced through those sections and came up with a few options for us to consider. Which one should we go with?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: You chose the following option. Why did you select that one?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I am leaning towards **"How do economic conditions influence housing insecurity?"** The authors repeatedly emphasized economic conditions, introduced two economic hypotheses, and examined whether changes in those conditions were associated with changes in homelessness.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: Agreed! I can see why some of the other choices might sound right—they use ideas that appear in the study. But they either focus on just one piece of the study or ask about something the researchers weren’t actually investigating. This question brings together the economic conditions they examined with the homelessness outcome they were trying to explain.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Great! I went ahead and added **"How do economic conditions influence housing insecurity?"** to our table.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: I bet we can locate clues for Evidence Used and Methods in the Method section of the source text. Why don’t we each read that section and highlight clues?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: Sounds good to me. Evidence used refers to data they collected and Methods is how they collected that data. Right?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Yes, that is right. Go ahead and highlight text for Evidence Used and Methods.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: I highlighted **state-level panel data** which probably includes homelessness rates and data around entrepreneurial activity and labor market freedom indicators.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: For methods, I highlighted **Dynamic econometric methods** ... **Panel Vector Autoregression (PVAR), Granger causality testing, and Cholesky forecast-error variance decomposition**. It looks like these are the analytic methods they used to analyze that data.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Yes, that is right.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Great. I entered that information for Evidence used and Methods.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: Now we need to identify the Underlying Assumption.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: This is a little bit different. Underlying assumption is about the discipline and how it views and understands reality. It rarely appears in a research paper, but we can infer it from some of the rows in our table.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: That is very interesting. Let’s see if we can identify the underlying assumption of this discipline by looking at the phenomena researchers studied, the questions they asked, and the data and methods they used to analyze their evidence.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: So we need to look beyond what this particular study found and ask what these choices tell us about how economists tend to understand social problems.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: Right. This study focuses on markets, employment, economic opportunity, and institutions. That gives us clues about the broader Economics perspective behind the study.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Exactly. Those clues can help us infer the **underlying assumption** of the discipline.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
An underlying assumption is a **broad belief about how a discipline understands the reality**. It is not the finding of one particular study.

A good disciplinary assumption sentence:

- Describes how the discipline understands reality
- Can guide many studies in the discipline
- Is not the conclusion of one particular study
- Could appear in the introduction of a textbook in that discipline

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Let’s test these criteria with the study main insight: **Higher levels of entrepreneurial activity and labor market freedom may reduce homelessness by expanding economic opportunity and reducing barriers to employment.**

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text:
I marked **No** for all the criteria. I don’t think our main insight passes the test. It tells us what this particular study found about entrepreneurial activity, labor market freedom, and homelessness. It doesn't describe a broad way that Economics understands the world, nor does it apply across many Economics studies.

| **Does the study's main insight...** | **Yes** | **No** |
|---|---|---|
| Describe how Economics generally understands reality? |   | ✓ |
| Apply broadly across many Economics studies? |   | ✓ |
| Go beyond the findings of this particular study? |   | ✓ |
| Sound like something we might read in an introductory Economics textbook? |   | ✓ |

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: So, we need to step back from the study's finding and look for the broader idea behind it?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Exactly! We need to step back from the particular findings and think about what broader ideas about the world seem to guide this study. Think about the phenomena the researchers studied, the question they pursued, and the main insight their study offers.

Here are some options. Which statement turns those clues into a broader assumption of Economics?

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: I like **“Economic systems, incentives, and institutional conditions influence human behavior and social outcomes**.” Unlike the other options, this sentence describes a broad assumption of the Economics discipline, not the findings of this particular study. It explains how economists generally understand the world—that economic systems, incentives, and institutions influence human behavior and social outcomes.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: Exactly! Notice also that this idea could guide many different economics studies and could easily appear in the opening chapter of an Economics textbook. The Cebula and Saunoris study is one example of researchers applying this broader disciplinary assumption to investigate homelessness.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: That is right! I went ahead and entered it on our table.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Before we move on to our next disciplinary source, let's pause for a moment.

We've spent some time exploring how the Economics discipline approaches housing insecurity. Take a minute to think about what you've learned so far.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text:
I used the search term method and found another study on homelessness.

This one focuses on income support policies and family homelessness. Take a look.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Which discipline do you think is most representative of this study?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Can you show us why? Highlight at least 5 keywords that link this study to the discipline you selected.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I chose **Public Policy**. The most important clue for me was the phenomena they studied: **income support policies, public assistance programs, and their relation to housing stability.**

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Exactly! These are all phenomena Public Policy researchers study to understand how government programs and policy choices affect people’s lives. Nicely done.

As we did with the previous source, we now need to identify the main “insight” of this study.

Remember, a study insight is usually the main finding, explanation, or recommendation offered by the authors. It reflects how the discipline explains the problem.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: When we did that for the first study, we honed in on the Results, Discussion, and Conclusion sections.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: We should do the same thing and highlight sentences in those three sections that may offer clues about the main insight of this study.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Let’s do it. Highlight 2–3 sentences that give us the strongest clues about the study's main insight.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: These are the sentences I highlighted. They tell us what the study found about TANF and what that finding means: greater access to direct cash assistance may reduce family homelessness, showing that income support policy can influence housing stability.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: Thanks Ty. These are very similar to what I highlighted.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text:
Yeah, thanks, Ty. I think there are great clues in your highlights.

Now look across these highlighted sentences.

In your own words, what do you think is the **main insight of this study?**

Try to capture more than a single result. Think about what the researchers want us to understand from the study as a whole.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Good work. Here are the sentences you all suggested. Which one should we go with?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: You chose the following sentence. Why did you select that one?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: I picked “**Public policy design, particularly access to direct cash assistance, can play an important role in reducing family homelessness.”**

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: Can you explain why?

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text:
Sure. Notice how this explanation centers on government policies, public programs, and access to resources. Those ideas reflect the perspective of the Public Policy discipline.

The study also found that these effects were especially strong in majority–Black and Native American school districts.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: I agree. Thanks for that discussion. Let's add the Parolin study to our table. I already entered the phenomena studied and the study’s main insight. We still need to identify the remaining rows.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: For Questions Asked, let’s look at the Abstract, Introduction and Background sections. Those are sections we read for clues when we did this for the first source.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: Here are some suggestions. Which of these should we go with?

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: You chose the following option. Why did you select that one?

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: The study focuses on whether differences in the accessibility and generosity of income support programs are related to family homelessness. That makes **“How do income support policies influence family homelessness?”** the best match for the researchers’ central question.

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: That makes sense.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: I agree. I added it to our table. Let’s work on filling out the rest of the rows for this study.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: It looks like for evidence they used **administrative data on student homelessness from public school districts with measures of state-level income support policy generosity and accessibility.**

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text: And they did an analysis of **cross-state and over-time differences in program access and generosity.**

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Go ahead and highlight text for Evidence Used and Methods.

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: Great. I entered those in our table for evidence used and methods. That leaves us with the underlying assumption.

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: How about “**Access to government cash assistance can improve housing stability for low-income families”?**

body.speaker: Lianne
body.text: That certainly fits this study. But is it broad enough to be an underlying assumption of the Public Policy discipline? Let’s check against our criteria.

body.speaker: Peggy
body.text:
This is how I answered them. It tells us something important, but it stays too close to this particular study—cash assistance, housing stability, and low-income families. We need to move up a level and ask what broader belief about policy and society seems to guide the study.

| **Criteria** | **Yes** | **No** |
|---|---|---|
| Describes how the discipline understands reality |   | ✓ |
| Can guide many studies in the discipline |   | ✓ |
| Is not the conclusion of this particular study |   | ✓ |
| Could appear in an introductory Public Policy textbook |   | ✓ |

body.speaker: Ty
body.text: What if we broaden it to “**Government policies and institutions shape social conditions and people’s opportunities”?**

body.speaker: Lacy
body.text: That seems different. It isn’t just about TANF or homelessness anymore. Let’s see if this one passes our criteria.

Title: When Climate Meets Real Estate: A Survey of the Literature
Authors: Justin Contat, Carrie Hopkins, Luis Mejia, & Matthew Suandi
Journal: Real Estate Economics
Publication Year: 2024
Volume/Issue/Pages: 52(3), 618–659
DOI: 10.1111/1540-6229.12489

Abstract
This article surveys research examining how climate change affects real estate and housing markets. The review synthesizes findings on physical climate risks—including flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, and sea level rise—as well as transition risks associated with decarbonization and energy policy. Across studies, climate-related environmental hazards were found to influence property values, insurance costs, mortgage lending, migration patterns, and housing affordability. The review highlights how climate-related disruptions may contribute to housing instability and disproportionate impacts on economically vulnerable communities.

Introduction
Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity, and geographic reach of environmental hazards such as flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, and extreme weather events. Because housing and real estate are directly tied to physical environments, climate-related risks increasingly shape housing markets and residential stability. This article examines how climate risks affect housing systems, real estate markets, and patterns of housing vulnerability.

Background
Previous research on housing instability and homelessness has often focused on poverty, unemployment, housing supply, and social policy. However, growing research suggests that climate-related environmental hazards may also contribute to housing precarity by damaging housing infrastructure, increasing insurance costs, reducing property values in high-risk areas, and displacing residents following environmental disasters. Researchers have increasingly examined how environmental risks become incorporated into real estate and housing markets.

Method
This article presents a
large-scale survey of academic literature

examining how climate-related environmental risks affect real estate and housing markets. The authors reviewed empirical research across multiple areas of climate risk, organizing the literature into two broad categories: physical climate risks and transition risks. Physical risks included hazards such as flooding, hurricanes, sea level rise, wildfire exposure, and extreme weather events, while transition risks focused on energy efficiency regulations, decarbonization policies, and changing environmental market expectations.
Across the reviewed studies, researchers commonly relied on
longitudinal housing market data, geospatial climate-risk mapping, mortgage and insurance records, migration data, and econometric modeling techniques
to examine relationships among environmental hazards, housing prices, lending outcomes, insurance availability, and housing affordability. The article
synthesized findings from both quantitative and qualitative studies

to identify major patterns connecting climate risk and housing instability.

Results
The literature reviewed identified consistent evidence that climate-related environmental hazards increasingly shape housing markets and housing stability. Across multiple studies, properties exposed to flood risk experienced measurable declines in housing values once environmental risks became publicly visible through updated flood maps, disaster exposure, or disclosure policies. For example, one study reviewed found that homes newly assigned to flood zones experienced approximately an 11% decrease in property prices following changes in flood risk mapping. Other studies reported that repeated flood exposure contributed to declining housing demand and lower long-term property values in high-risk areas.
Research on hurricanes, severe storms, and wildfire exposure similarly found disruptions to local housing markets, increased insurance costs, and longer-term displacement pressures for affected populations. Several studies reviewed reported increased mortgage delinquency risks and worsening financial outcomes among households affected by flooding and climate-related disasters. One study discussed in the review found that, outside protected floodplain areas, flood exposure was associated with a 20% increase in bankruptcies and a 13% increase in severe debt delinquency among credit-constrained homeowners.
The review also found evidence that climate risks increasingly influence migration and residential decision-making. Households with greater financial resources were often more capable of relocating away from environmentally vulnerable areas, while lower-income populations experienced greater difficulty recovering from environmental disasters or relocating to safer housing markets. As a result, climate-related housing instability disproportionately affected economically vulnerable populations.
Across the literature, environmental risks were increasingly found to shape housing affordability, insurance availability, lending decisions, migration patterns, and long-term residential stability. The authors argue that climate change is becoming an increasingly important factor in understanding housing precarity and displacement.

Discussion
The findings suggest that climate change affects housing systems not only through direct environmental destruction, but also through economic and market processes that shape housing stability. Environmental hazards may alter where people can afford to live, increase displacement pressures, and intensify housing precarity for already vulnerable populations. The article argues that climate vulnerability should be considered an increasingly important factor in housing stability and homelessness prevention efforts.

Conclusion
Climate-related environmental hazards such as flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, and sea level rise increasingly shape housing markets, affordability, displacement, and housing stability. The growing interaction between climate systems and housing markets highlights the importance of understanding homelessness and housing precarity not only as economic or social issues, but also as problems shaped by environmental risk and climate vulnerability.

**Title:** When Climate Meets Real Estate: A Survey of the Literature  
**Authors:** Justin Contat, Carrie Hopkins, Luis Mejia, & Matthew Suandi  
**Journal:** Real Estate Economics  
**Publication Year:** 2024  
**Volume/Issue/Pages:** 52(3), 618–659  
**DOI:** 10.1111/1540-6229.12489  

#### Abstract

This article surveys research examining how climate change affects real estate and housing markets. The review synthesizes findings on physical climate risks—including flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, and sea level rise—as well as transition risks associated with decarbonization and energy policy. Across studies, climate-related environmental hazards were found to influence property values, insurance costs, mortgage lending, migration patterns, and housing affordability. The review highlights how climate-related disruptions may contribute to housing instability and disproportionate impacts on economically vulnerable communities.

#### Introduction

Climate change is increasing the frequency, intensity, and geographic reach of environmental hazards such as flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, and extreme weather events. Because housing and real estate are directly tied to physical environments, climate-related risks increasingly shape housing markets and residential stability. This article examines how climate risks affect housing systems, real estate markets, and patterns of housing vulnerability.

#### Background

Previous research on housing instability and homelessness has often focused on poverty, unemployment, housing supply, and social policy. However, growing research suggests that climate-related environmental hazards may also contribute to housing precarity by damaging housing infrastructure, increasing insurance costs, reducing property values in high-risk areas, and displacing residents following environmental disasters. Researchers have increasingly examined how environmental risks become incorporated into real estate and housing markets.

#### Method

This article presents a large-scale survey of academic literature examining how climate-related environmental risks affect real estate and housing markets. The authors reviewed empirical research across multiple areas of climate risk, organizing the literature into two broad categories: physical climate risks and transition risks. Physical risks included hazards such as flooding, hurricanes, sea level rise, wildfire exposure, and extreme weather events, while transition risks focused on energy efficiency regulations, decarbonization policies, and changing environmental market expectations.

Across the reviewed studies, researchers commonly relied on longitudinal housing market data, geospatial climate-risk mapping, mortgage and insurance records, migration data, and econometric modeling techniques to examine relationships among environmental hazards, housing prices, lending outcomes, insurance availability, and housing affordability. The article synthesized findings from both quantitative and qualitative studies to identify major patterns connecting climate risk and housing instability.

#### Results

The literature reviewed identified consistent evidence that climate-related environmental hazards increasingly shape housing markets and housing stability. Across multiple studies, properties exposed to flood risk experienced measurable declines in housing values once environmental risks became publicly visible through updated flood maps, disaster exposure, or disclosure policies. For example, one study reviewed found that homes newly assigned to flood zones experienced approximately an 11% decrease in property prices following changes in flood risk mapping. Other studies reported that repeated flood exposure contributed to declining housing demand and lower long-term property values in high-risk areas.

Research on hurricanes, severe storms, and wildfire exposure similarly found disruptions to local housing markets, increased insurance costs, and longer-term displacement pressures for affected populations. Several studies reviewed reported increased mortgage delinquency risks and worsening financial outcomes among households affected by flooding and climate-related disasters. One study discussed in the review found that, outside protected floodplain areas, flood exposure was associated with a 20% increase in bankruptcies and a 13% increase in severe debt delinquency among credit-constrained homeowners.

The review also found evidence that climate risks increasingly influence migration and residential decision-making. Households with greater financial resources were often more capable of relocating away from environmentally vulnerable areas, while lower-income populations experienced greater difficulty recovering from environmental disasters or relocating to safer housing markets. As a result, climate-related housing instability disproportionately affected economically vulnerable populations.

Across the literature, environmental risks were increasingly found to shape housing affordability, insurance availability, lending decisions, migration patterns, and long-term residential stability. The authors argue that climate change is becoming an increasingly important factor in understanding housing precarity and displacement.

#### Discussion

The findings suggest that climate change affects housing systems not only through direct environmental destruction, but also through economic and market processes that shape housing stability. Environmental hazards may alter where people can afford to live, increase displacement pressures, and intensify housing precarity for already vulnerable populations. The article argues that climate vulnerability should be considered an increasingly important factor in housing stability and homelessness prevention efforts.

#### Conclusion

Climate-related environmental hazards such as flooding, hurricanes, wildfires, and sea level rise increasingly shape housing markets, affordability, displacement, and housing stability. The growing interaction between climate systems and housing markets highlights the importance of understanding homelessness and housing precarity not only as economic or social issues, but also as problems shaped by environmental risk and climate vulnerability.

Thank you for participating in this focus group and for providing your consent to have this meeting recorded. §
Our community needs survey identified homelessness as an issue of concern. § The purpose of this focus group is to discuss causes of homelessness in our community. §
Why do you think people in our community lose stable housing? §

Participant 1 (Longtime Resident) §
I’ve lived here for over twenty years, and what I’ve noticed is that the cost of living has changed dramatically. §
Rent has gone up steadily, but wages haven’t kept pace.

§ I know families where both adults are working full time, but nearly half their income goes to housing. §
When rent increases by even a few hundred dollars, that’s not just an inconvenience — that can completely destabilize a household budget. § There’s very little room for error. §

Participant 2 (Small Business Owner) §
I see that in my own workplace. § Some of my employees are reliable and hardworking, but they don’t have savings to fall back on. § When something unexpected happens — a medical bill, car trouble, reduced hours — they can’t absorb the shock. §
It’s not that they’re irresponsible. §
It’s that their financial margins are so thin that one setback becomes a housing crisis.

§

Interviewer §
Thank you. § For now, let’s focus specifically on the causes that lead to losing housing. § We’ll discuss possible supports later. §

Participant 3 (Person Currently Experiencing Homelessness) §
For me, it started with job loss. §
I worked in hospitality for years. § When the pandemic hit, I was laid off. § I used my savings to cover rent for as long as I could, thinking things would bounce back quickly. § But savings run out faster than you think when there’s no income coming in. §
When I found work again, it paid less and offered fewer hours. § I was already behind. § Once the eviction notice was filed, it felt like the damage was done. §
Even after I moved out, that eviction followed me.
I’ve filled out applications since then, and landlords see that record and move on to the next applicant.

§
It wasn’t one bad decision. § It was a series of events without a safety net. §

Participant 4 (Community Service Provider) §
What you described reflects what we see regularly. §

§

Participant 5 (Housing Advocate) §
I’d also emphasize structural factors. §

Zoning restrictions, neighborhood resistance to new developments, and rising construction costs all contribute to limited supply.

§
When demand exceeds supply, rents increase. § That’s basic economics. § But the result is that lower-income renters are constantly competing for fewer available units. §

Participant 3 §

When you’re exhausted, it’s harder to search for jobs, keep appointments, or think clearly.

§

Legal barriers also play a significant role. §

§

I’d also mention income support programs. §
Some families lose benefits because of small technical issues — paperwork errors, missing deadlines, small changes in income that disqualify them.
When assistance stops suddenly, there’s no cushion.

§

#### Interviewer

Thank you for participating in this focus group and for providing your consent to have this meeting recorded.

Our community needs survey identified homelessness as an issue of concern. The purpose of this focus group is to discuss causes of homelessness in our community.

Why do you think people in our community lose stable housing?

I’ve lived here for over twenty years, and what I’ve noticed is that **the cost of living has changed dramatically. Rent has gone up steadily, but wages haven’t kept pace.** I know families where both adults are working full time, but nearly half their income goes to housing.

#### Participant 2 (Small Business Owner)

I see that in my own workplace. Some of my employees are reliable and hardworking, but they don’t have savings to fall back on. When something unexpected happens — a medical bill, car trouble, reduced hours — they can’t absorb the shock.

It’s not that they’re irresponsible. **It’s that their financial margins are so thin that one setback becomes a housing crisis.**

#### Interviewer

Thank you. For now, let’s focus specifically on the causes that lead to losing housing. We’ll discuss possible supports later.

#### Participant 3 (Person Currently Experiencing Homelessness)

For me, it started with job loss.

I worked in hospitality for years. When the pandemic hit, I was laid off. I used my savings to cover rent for as long as I could, thinking things would bounce back quickly. But savings run out faster than you think when there’s no income coming in.

When I found work again, it paid less and offered fewer hours. I was already behind. Once the eviction notice was filed, it felt like the damage was done. **Even after I moved out, that eviction followed me. I’ve filled out applications since then, and landlords see that record and move on to the next applicant.**

It wasn’t one bad decision. It was a series of events without a safety net.

#### Participant 4 (Community Service Provider)

What you described reflects what we see regularly.

**Many people we serve have experienced trauma — domestic violence, family conflict, untreated mental health conditions. Those experiences can disrupt employment, relationships, and stability.**

Housing loss is often the final stage of a longer period of stress and instability. By the time someone seeks help, they’ve already exhausted informal supports like friends and family.

#### Participant 5 (Housing Advocate)

I’d also emphasize structural factors.

**In this region, affordable housing development hasn’t kept up with population growth. Zoning restrictions, neighborhood resistance to new developments, and rising construction costs all contribute to limited supply.**

When demand exceeds supply, rents increase. That’s basic economics. But the result is that lower-income renters are constantly competing for fewer available units.

Even people who have stable employment can be priced out.

#### Participant 3

And once someone becomes unsheltered, things can deteriorate quickly.

Last summer, during the heat wave, I was sleeping in my car. **The heat made it hard to rest. I was constantly fatigued and dehydrated. When you’re exhausted, it’s harder to search for jobs, keep appointments, or think clearly.**

Homelessness itself creates new barriers.

#### Participant 6 (Legal Aid Worker)

Legal barriers also play a significant role.

**An eviction filing — even if someone eventually pays what they owe — often appears in tenant screening databases. Many landlords automatically deny applications with prior eviction history.**

**Criminal records can create similar obstacles. Even minor charges can limit housing options.**

Once someone has that record, it narrows their choices considerably.

#### Participant 2

I’d also mention income support programs.

**Some families lose benefits because of small technical issues — paperwork errors, missing deadlines, small changes in income that disqualify them. When assistance stops suddenly, there’s no cushion.**

Without that financial floor, housing becomes fragile.

#### Interviewer

Are there any other comments on the causes? [Interviewer pause]

Okay, let’s move on to the next part of the focus group.

Title: Income Support Policies and the Rise of Student and Family Homelessness
Author: Zachary Parolin
Journal: The ANNALS of the American Academy of Political and Social Science
Publication Year: 2021
Volume/Issue/Pages: 693(1), 46–63
DOI: 10.1177/0002716220981847

Abstract (Summary)
This study examines whether the generosity and accessibility of publicly provided income support policies influence levels of family and student homelessness in the United States. Using administrative data on student homelessness across most U.S. public school districts and state-level variation in access to cash and near-cash assistance programs, the analysis assesses how differences in policy generosity are associated with homelessness rates. Findings indicate that greater access to TANF cash assistance is significantly associated with lower rates of family homelessness, particularly in districts with majority–Black or Native American student populations. Evidence for the effects of SNAP and EITC is inconclusive.

Introduction
Family homelessness has increased in the U.S. in recent years, as indicated by Department of Education data showing rising numbers of students experiencing homelessness. Traditional explanations emphasize housing costs and structural economic conditions, but this study focuses on how variation in income support policy design — specifically cash and near-cash assistance accessibility — may shape family homelessness outcomes.

Background
The U.S. welfare state includes multiple income support programs intended to raise economic resources for low-income families. Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) provides direct cash assistance, whereas the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) offers food support, and the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) provides wage subsidies for certain working families. Prior research suggests that income support reduces economic hardship, but less is known about how variation in policy generosity and access affects homelessness specifically.

Method
The analysis combines
administrative data on student homelessness from public school districts
with
measures of state-level income support policy generosity and accessibility
. Focus is placed on three major programs: TANF, SNAP, and the EITC. Using
cross-state and over-time differences in program access and generosity

, the study estimates how these variations relate to differences in homelessness rates among students and families with children.

Results
Greater access to cash assistance through TANF is associated with significantly lower rates of family homelessness. Increases in the accessibility of TANF cash benefits correspond with measurable declines in family homelessness rates. The negative association between TANF access and homelessness is particularly pronounced in majority–Black and Native American school districts. In contrast, greater access to SNAP benefits does not show a consistent relationship with reduced homelessness, and increased generosity of the EITC yields inconclusive effects on homelessness levels.

Discussion
These findings suggest that direct cash assistance may play a distinctive role in reducing family homelessness, beyond what in-kind (SNAP) or conditional wage subsidy (EITC) programs achieve. The study highlights how policy retrenchment — particularly declines in TANF accessibility — may help explain recent trends in homelessness among families with children. It also underscores the importance of considering racial and ethnic disparities in program effects.

Conclusion
Family and student homelessness in the U.S. is associated with the accessibility of income support policies. Greater access to cash assistance through TANF is linked to lower homelessness rates, suggesting that policy design within the welfare state influences housing stability. SNAP and EITC do not show clear protective associations in this study. Integrating income support policy into homelessness research provides a broader understanding of structural determinants of housing insecurity.

Title: Racialized Homelessness: A Review of Historical and Contemporary Causes of Racial Disparities in Homelessness
Author: Matthew Z. Fowle
Journal: Housing Policy Debate
Publication Year: 2022
DOI: 10.1080/10511482.2022.2026995
Link: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10511482.2022.2026995

Abstract (Summary)
This article synthesizes historical and contemporary scholarship to explain why homelessness in the United States is disproportionately concentrated among Black, Latinx, and Native American populations. Rather than treating homelessness as race-neutral or reducible to individual deficits, the review frames homelessness as a racialized outcome produced through structural racism operating across housing, economic, political, and social institutions. The article argues that racial disparities in homelessness are closely tied to long-standing patterns of housing discrimination, residential segregation, economic inequality, and unequal treatment within homelessness response systems. The review concludes that meaningful reductions in homelessness disparities require structural reforms that confront these interconnected institutional systems.

Introduction
Despite representing a smaller proportion of the overall U.S. population, Black, Latinx, and Native American individuals are disproportionately represented among people experiencing homelessness. The article examines why these racial disparities persist and argues that explanations focused only on poverty, mental health, or individual behavior are insufficient. Instead, the review situates homelessness within broader historical and sociological processes involving racial exclusion, segregation, and institutional inequality.

Background
Previous homelessness research has often emphasized factors such as housing affordability, unemployment, mental illness, and service availability. However, this article argues that less attention has been given to how racial stratification shapes exposure to these risks. Drawing from sociological and historical scholarship, the review traces how discriminatory housing and economic systems have constrained wealth accumulation, residential stability, and access to safe housing for communities of color across generations.

Method
This article uses a
sociological literature review

approach to synthesize historical and contemporary research on racial disparities in homelessness. The author reviewed scholarship from sociology, housing studies, economics, public policy, and homelessness research to identify recurring structural patterns associated with racialized homelessness. The review draws on
demographic homelessness statistics, historical housing policy analyses, segregation research, eviction studies, housing discrimination research, and studies of homeless service systems

. Rather than relying on a single dataset or experiment, the article compares findings across multiple studies to examine how institutional systems interact to shape homelessness outcomes over time.

Results / Findings
The reviewed research consistently found that homelessness disproportionately affects Black, Native American, and Latinx populations in the United States. Several studies cited in the article reported that Black Americans make up approximately 13% of the U.S. population but nearly 40% of the homeless population nationally. Research reviewed in the article also found that Black individuals are more likely to experience unsheltered homelessness and longer durations of homelessness than White individuals.
Across the reviewed scholarship, racial disparities persisted even when controlling for poverty, suggesting that economic hardship alone does not fully explain homelessness disparities. The review repeatedly identified structural factors such as residential segregation, discriminatory lending and rental practices, eviction disparities, unequal access to housing wealth, and disproportionate criminal legal system involvement as major contributors to housing instability among communities of color.
Historical analyses reviewed in the article connected present-day homelessness disparities to long-term institutional processes such as redlining, racially restrictive covenants, urban renewal displacement, discriminatory welfare policies, and exclusion from wealth-building housing opportunities.

Discussion
The article argues that homelessness cannot be fully understood through individual-level explanations alone because racial inequality is embedded across multiple institutional systems. From a sociological perspective, homelessness is viewed as a structural outcome shaped by historical and contemporary systems of power, inequality, and exclusion. The review suggests that homelessness policies focused only on shelters or emergency services are unlikely to eliminate racial disparities unless broader inequalities in housing access, wealth accumulation, criminal legal exposure, and social policy are also addressed.

Conclusion
The article concludes that homelessness in the United States is deeply shaped by structural racism operating across housing, economic, and political systems. Reducing racial disparities in homelessness requires structural reforms such as enforcing fair housing protections, reducing discriminatory housing practices, expanding affordable housing access, addressing racial wealth gaps, and reforming institutional systems that contribute to unequal housing vulnerability.

Title: “It Wasn’t Just One Thing”: A Qualitative Study of Newly Homeless Emergency Department Patients
Authors: Kelly M. Doran, Ziwei Ran, Donna Castelblanco, Donna Shelley, & Deborah K. Padgett
Journal: Academic Emergency Medicine
Publication Year: 2019
Volume/Issue/Pages: 26(9), 982–993
DOI: 10.1111/acem.13677
Link: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6732033/

Abstract
This qualitative study examines how social relationships, life experiences, and structural conditions interact to shape pathways into homelessness. Through in-depth interviews with individuals who had become homeless within the previous six months, the researchers found that homelessness rarely resulted from one isolated event. Instead, participants described interconnected social processes involving job loss, health problems, family conflict, relationship breakdown, unaffordable housing, mental health challenges, substance use, and limited social support. The study concludes that homelessness develops through the cumulative interaction of personal, relational, and structural factors across people's lives.

Introduction
Research on homelessness often identifies factors such as poverty, mental illness, unemployment, or housing costs as separate causes of homelessness. This study takes a different approach by examining how multiple social conditions and life experiences interact over time. Rather than asking which single factor causes homelessness, the researchers explore how people understand the social pathways that led to their housing instability.

Background
Previous research has identified many risk factors associated with homelessness, including unemployment, housing shortages, domestic violence, poor health, and mental illness. However, less research has examined how these factors interact within people's lived experiences and social relationships. The authors argue that homelessness is better understood as the result of layered personal, relational, and structural challenges that accumulate over time rather than as the consequence of any single event.

Method
Researchers conducted
semi-structured qualitative interviews

with 31 emergency department patients who had become homeless within the previous six months. Participants described their employment histories, housing experiences, family and social relationships, health challenges, financial stressors, and support systems. Rather than using statistical analysis, the researchers analyzed participants' narratives to identify recurring social patterns, relationships, and pathways into homelessness.

Results
Participants consistently described homelessness as the result of interacting social, economic, health, and relational challenges rather than one isolated event. Researchers identified four recurring themes:
Homelessness developed through multiple interacting problems.
Family relationships and social support networks often weakened or became exhausted.
Participants struggled to balance personal responsibility with larger structural barriers.
Homelessness emerged through cascading pathways in which problems accumulated over time.
Across participants, common pathways included job loss, illness, family conflict, domestic violence, mental health struggles, rising housing costs, unstable employment, and weak social support systems. Participants frequently described homelessness as "everything piling up" rather than the result of one poor decision.

Discussion
The findings suggest that homelessness is produced through the interaction of personal experiences, social relationships, and broader structural conditions. By examining participants' lived experiences and personal narratives, the researchers demonstrate how employment instability, family relationships, housing pressures, health challenges, and support networks become interconnected over time. This sociological perspective helps explain homelessness as a social process rather than an isolated individual event.

Conclusion
Homelessness pathways are complex, cumulative, and socially interconnected. Qualitative interviews reveal how relationships, support systems, employment, housing conditions, health, and structural barriers combine to shape people's experiences of homelessness. Understanding these interacting social pathways can help researchers and policymakers develop more comprehensive responses to housing instability.
